items.item: General key-management guidance and best practices, the standards backing for this topic's vocabulary.
Pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data named as an appropriate security measure.
A DEK encrypts data locally; a KEK held in the KMS only ever wraps and unwraps the DEK, never touching the data itself.

at.step: Reveal: the DEK/KEK hierarchy — what the KMS actually sees

items.item: KEK rotation re-wraps DEKs with zero data re-encryption; a DEK compromise is a structurally different problem that forces re-encrypting every block under that DEK.

at.step: Reveal: rotation versus compromise

items.item: Provider-managed, customer-managed, BYOK and external key control form a single scale: more control trades directly against more availability risk (an external key manager's outage becomes a data outage).

at.step: Reveal: customer-managed, BYOK, external — a control-versus-availability scale

items.item: TLS and mTLS protect data in motion between two peers; they say nothing about data once it is written to disk, or about either endpoint's own security.

at.step: Reveal: TLS and mTLS — the wire, not the disk

items.item: Iceberg and Parquet both implement the same DEK/KEK envelope shape at the file format level, not just at the KMS level.

items.item: Crypto-shredding: destroying a key makes everything it encrypted unreadable everywhere without touching the data itself; the granularity of the key is the granularity of what gets erased, which topic 9 depends on directly.

items.item: Topic 4's tier/category tags are what a key hierarchy actually protects once applied; this topic assumes a column is already classified restricted before asking how to protect it.

NIST SP 800-57's own three-part structure (general guidance, government policy, cryptographic-feature usage) situates this topic's vocabulary within a wider standards document this topic does not fully cover.

The predict question's two parts (a leaked key under annual rotation; a request to make one subject's data unrecoverable) map directly onto this topic's two sharpest claims: rotation does not fix a leaked DEK, and key deletion is the crypto-shredding operation that answers the erasure question.
